DT is the amount of addi- tional python characters that a from-scratch model of the same size would have needed to achieve the same loss on python as a ﬁne-tuned model. In the labeled example, we see that for a 40M parameter transformer ﬁne-tuned on 3e5 characters, DT is approximately 1000x bigger than DF. The less ﬁne-tuning data is avail- able, the more pre-training helps. 1 Introduction Three factors drive the advance of AI: algorithmic innovation [HB20], compute [AH18], and data. OpenAI Five played over 10,000 years worth of Dota, AlphaZero played 140 million games of Go, and GPT-3 read a signiﬁcant fraction of the internet [OBB +19, SSS+17, BMR+20]. Those ML systems were all trained from-scratch, but humans “transfer” past understanding and experiences, which is part of what enables us to achieve impressive performance with much less direct experience at a task. The fact that neural networks often require more direct experience than a person can consume in a lifetime suggests that sample efﬁciency improvements that result from transfer might be an important way to characterize data. Recent progress in unsupervised and ﬁne-tuned language models makes them a particularly interesting do- main of study. Unsupervised pre-training improved downstream performance in [DL15] and enabled im- provements in data efﬁciency in [PNI +18, HR18]. The performance of the GPT-1 [RNSS18] transformer model [VSP+17] was boosted by pre-training. Later work leveraging ﬁne-tuning on small datasets has con- tinued to generate state of the art results [PNI +18, DCLT18, RSR+20]. This history of success suggests that language model ﬁne-tuning could provide a simple and interesting setting to study transfer between data distributions. We believe it is particularly important to characterize ﬁne-tuning in the low data regime because many tasks of interest won’t have a sufﬁciently big, readily available dataset to train large models from-scratch (either billions of data points [HNA+17, KMH+20, HKK+20] or a perfect simulator like in Go [SHM +16]). Fine- tuning a language model on code generation was particularly interesting to us because text and code have some overlap, but are fairly different distributions. Our analysis focuses on units of data while holding performance and model size constant. This novel lens allowed us to generate surprisingly clean ﬁts with the simple equation 1.1. 1.1 Key Results We train a series of transformer language models with a variety of sizes with 3 different dataset curricula: train from-scratch on python code, pre-train on natural language then ﬁne-tune on python code, and pre-train on an equal mix of natural language and non-python code then ﬁne-tune on python. We vary the size of the 3Pre-trained on Text Pre-trained on Text and other Programming Languages Figure 2 In the low-data regime, we observe a good ﬁt for over 4 orders of magnitude in model size and 3 orders of magnitude in ﬁne-tuning dataset size. The ﬁt equation is shown above in terms of DT for simplicity, but the fractional form is given by equation B.2. We show the omitted high data regime points in Appendix D. Details for the approach used to generate these ﬁts are shown in Appendix C. network and the ﬁne-tuning dataset, and measure the performance on a held-out test set of python code. We observe the following key results: The effective data transferred is well-described by a power-law in the low-data regime 2: We use DT to represent the effective data transferred, i.e. the amount of additional python data that a model of the same size trained on only python would have needed to achieve the same loss on python as a model pre-trained on language. Our notation is indicated visually in ﬁgure 1. The scaling law for transfer in equation 1.1 is at the core of many key insights and predictions in this work. We ﬁnd the simplicity of this result very intriguing: DT = effective data transferred = k(DF)α(N)β (1.1) where N is the number of non-embedding model parameters, and DF is the size of the ﬁne-tuning data distribution. When comparing pre-training on text and pre-training on an equal mix of text and non-python code 3 we found identical scaling with model size, the exponent β= 0.38 in equation 1.1. Thus the exponent beta appears to depend only on the model architecture and target distribution. We hypothesize that it measures how the model architecture generalizes on the target distribution. The quantity αprovides a useful measure of the directed proximity of two distributions, with smaller αindicating closer proximity. Measurements of αare cheap and enable one to make principled trade- offs between collecting expensive ﬁne-tuning data and increasing model size . Figure 2 shows that with very few experiments we can generate a relatively robust estimate of the transfer coefﬁcients. Potentially cheaper experiments are discussed in Section 6.3. For transfer from text to python we have β ≈2α, so increasing the data-set size by a factor, C, would be worth approximately the same as increasing the model size, N, by √ C. In other words, a 10x increase in model size, N, would be worth approximately a 100x increase in ﬁne-tuning dataset size, DF, under these conditions. The modest, ~10x, increase we see zero-shot from adding other programming languages into pre-training indicates that in our setting training on python is much better than training on other programming languages. This highlights the value of training entirely on one’s distribution of interest if possible. 2We deﬁne the low-data regime as having 10% or less of the amount of data it would take to get to 99% of the performance that inﬁnite data would yield. We show the details of estimating the data regime in Appendix A. 3The 50% text dataset is described in Section 2, and the 50% non-python code is 240 billion characters/340 GB, with the following components: 21% .c, 18% .java, 17% .js, 12% .cpp 7.6% php 6.5% .cs, 4.4% .md, 3.2% .cc, 3.2% .ts, 2.6% .go 1.8% .m, 1.7% .rb, .55% .sh. 4Transfer Coefﬁcients Transfer from k α β Text =⇒Python 1.9e4 0.18 0.38 50% Text and 50% non-python code =⇒Python 2.1e5 0.096 0.38 Table 1 Summary of transfer coefﬁcients . The larger k value indicates that mixture models transfer more readily than plain text in the low-data regime, while the smaller αmeans the beneﬁt diminishes as we approach the high-data regime. An implication of Equation 1.1 is that pre-training effectively multiplies the ﬁne-tuning dataset, DF , in the low-data regime .4 We ﬁnd the multiplier formulation helpful in building intuition. Note that the multiplier goes down as DF increases. effective data multiplier = DF + DT DF ≈DT DF = k(N)β (DF)1−α (1.2) When data is limiting performance, the pre-trained models have a better scaling law, in that the slope is less than zero: Figure 3 shows that as we increase model size with a ﬁxed amount DF of python data to ﬁnetune on, models trained from scratch hit a wall while models that were pre-trained on language continue to improve. Equations 1.1 and 1.2 quantify this phenomena. change in slopechange in slope data constraineddata constrained parameter constrainedparameter constrained Trained from Scratch Pre-trained on Text Figure 3 We observe large ﬂat regions where the from-scratch models are entirely data constrained (purple and blue lines) and get no beneﬁt from increased parameters, whereas the ﬁne-tuned scaling laws display only a change in slope when they are data-limited (green lines). A variant of these graphs with dataset size on the x-axis is shown in Section 3.1. Fits are by dataset size and have the functional form of power-laws plus constants. An attempt to ﬁt global power-laws to this data can be found in Appendix C. Zero-shot performance is given by the black line. Ignoring pre-training, ﬁne-tuned models are more compute efﬁcient in the low data regime (Figure 4). Ignoring the cost of pre-training makes sense when leveraging an existing pre-trained model like BERT or GPT-3 [DCLT18, BMR+20]. 4In the low data regime the effective data from transfer is much greater than the amount of data ﬁne-tuned on,DT >> DF . As a result, the total effective data, DE = DF + DT ≈DT , 5Pre-trained on Text Trained from Scratch Pre-trained pareto frontier Pre-trained pareto frontier Figure 4 In the low data regime, ﬁne-tuning gets better performance than training from scratch for a given amount of training compute and it’s much easier to be on the compute efﬁcient frontier. The performance gap widens severely as the model size grows with a ﬁxed amount of python. (Curves for 3e8 python characters) 1.2 Notation • DE - total effective data, the amount of python, in characters, that a model trained on python from- scratch of the same size would have needed to achieve the same loss on python as a pre-trained model. • DF - ﬁne-tuning dataset size, in characters • DT - effective data transferred, the amount of additional python, in characters, that a model trained on python from-scratch of the same size would have needed to achieve the same loss on python as a pre-trained model. • N - the number of model parameters, excluding vocabulary and positional embeddings. • α, β- power-law exponents for scaling of effective data transferred. • k- constant for scaling of effective data transferred. • L- the cross-entropy loss in nats per token, averaged over the tokens in a context. • C- the units of compute throughout the paper are ﬂoating point operations. • D(N) - the amount of data it takes to get 99% of the performance that inﬁnite python data would yield for a given model size. • αN, αD - power-law exponents for the loss L from [KMH+20]. • DC, NC - constants for the loss from [KMH+20]. 2 Methods The models pre-trained on language, ﬁne-tuned on code, and trained on code from-scratch were all trained to convergence to the optimal early stopping point, with learning rates and optimization parameters similar to those from [KMH+20]. Model size and dataset size each spanned 4 orders of magnitude. We used adam, [KB14] a batch size of 256, sequences of 2048 tokens, a 3000 step warm-up, and a vocabulary size of 50257. Pre-trained text models were trained on a mix of WebText2 described in [KMH +20], Common Crawl 5 [RSR+20], English Wikipedia, and publicly available Internet Books. The text was encoded with the re- versible tokenizer described in [RWC+19] for a total of 24 billion characters. Models trained or ﬁne-tuned on python leveraged a 22 billion character dataset sourced from public GitHub 6 repositories (31GB), with 3% of the data-set held out for evaluation. 5https://commoncrawl.org/the-data/ 6https://www.gharchive.org/ 63 Results 3.1 Ossiﬁcation – can pre-training harm performance? Can pre-training ever hurt the performance of a ﬁne-tuned model? We refer to this phenomenon as ‘ossi- ﬁcation,’ to suggest that pre-training can ossify the model weights so that they don’t adapt as well to the ﬁne-tuning distribution in the high data regime.. A variant of Figure 3 summarizing the experiments with data-set size on the x-axis rather than as the line color is shown below. To build intuition, it’s helpful to view the main results through several lenses. It is somewhat easier on this graph to observe that the smallest from-scratch models have better performance with large datasets than our ﬁne-tuned models with large datasets (purple lines). Trained from Scratch Pre-trained on Text Figure 5 In the high data regime (purple lines), pre-training can effectively reduce the training set size. In other words, we get better performance training the 1M parameter models (purple) with our larger size datasets (>1e8) from-scratch. We deﬁne D(N) as the amount of data it takes to reach 99% of the performance7 that inﬁnite python data would yield for a given model size. We then use fraction of D(N) to parameterize the data regime. We deﬁne D/D(N) <0.10 as the low data regime. We estimate D(N) to be similar for pre-trained and from-scratch models. See appendix A for the methodology we used to estimate D(N) and ﬁt of D(N) to our data. Throughout this work, we focus on the data-limited regime, because that is when pre-training is of most practical use. When D/D(N) approaches 1.0 we observe that pre-training reduces our effective data, and our small ﬁne-tuned models were unable to reach trained form scratch performance even as they were trained on 10x or 100x D(N). We refer to this phenomenon as ossiﬁcation because one could think of the pre-training as a particularly bad initialization that the model has trouble recovering from. It’s possible that with sufﬁcient tweaking/tuning we could recover from the poor initialization, but we didn’t investigate that question. It’s entirely possible that large models would have different behavior in this regime. 3.2 Fine-tuning is usually compute efﬁcient (ignoring pre-training compute) When we have approximately 30x more data than we had in Figure 4, the compute efﬁcient frontier for ﬁne- tuning is similar to that of from-scratch models. However, it’s much easier to be on the compute efﬁcient frontier when ﬁne-tuning. As shown in Figure 7, the training curves for ﬁne-tuning lie tangent to the frontier for most of training, while the from-scratch curves only lie tangent to the frontier for a relatively narrow window. 7Speciﬁcally, 0.99 times the loss given D(N) amount of data should equal the loss the model would have in the inﬁnite data regime, L(D →∞) = 0.99 ∗L(D(N)) 7Pre-training helpsPre-training helps Baseline: from scratch with D(N)Baseline: from scratch with D(N) Baseline: from scratch with D(N)Baseline: from scratch with D(N) Pre-training hurtsPre-training hurts hurtshurtshelpshelps 700M zero-shot700M zero-shot Data Multiplier vs Data Regime Fraction Effective Data from  Transfer vs Data Regime data multiplier from transfer fraction effective data from transfer Figure 6 Pre-training reduced effective data for small models in the high data regime. The graph on the right is a re-parameterization of graph on the left. Note: the parallelism of the purple curves and from-scratch D(N) baseline in orange relies on D(N), for which we had a noisy ﬁt as shown in Appendix A. Pre-trained on Text Trained from Scratch Figure 7 We show training curves for training on a 10B-character python dataset, parameterized by the amount of compute used for training. However, as shown with the smallest models in Section 3.1, once we start to have as much or more data than we’d want for training from scratch, ﬁne-tuning gets substantially worse converged performance and as such is also less compute efﬁcient. Many models are trained to convergence (compute is used until performance gains stop) rather than the efﬁ- cient compute frontier (pareto frontier for performance and compute) [KMH+20]. In ﬁgure 8 we summarize each curve above with a single point, the converged compute, so we can simultaneously view all the models we trained on datasets of varying size. When training to convergence: 1. Pre-trained models are more compute efﬁcient than training from-scratch given a small dataset 2. It’s easier to be on the compute frontier when ﬁne-tuning as compared to training from scratch, for any given dataset size. 8Pre-trained on Text Trained from Scratch Figure 8 Different points in a given color here all represent models of a given size trained to convergence on different sized datasets. An analysis of best epoch, which offers another lens on converged compute costs is given in Appendix G. 4 Related Work Power-laws can arise from a wide variety of sources [THK18]. Predictable scaling trends in neural networks were ﬁrst studied with [HNA +17]. The work closest to our approach is [RRBS19, KMH +20, HKK+20]. Our focus was on how transfer scales with compute, data, and parameters rather than how performance scales based on those ingredients when training from scratch. Transfer and meta-learning have received a lot of attention from the research community in many modalities. We will review some of the work that helped motivate us, but won’t do a comprehensive literature review. Here are two recent literature reviews in the domain. [TSK+18, Wen18]. We discussed pre-training language models in the introduction. Pre-training on image datasets such as Insta- gram and ImageNet has also produced gains in overall performance and data efﬁciency [MGR+18, HGD19]. CLIP showed impressive transfer from captioned images by getting zero-shot accuracy comparable to a ResNet-50 on ImageNet on datasets like ImageNet A [RKH+, DDS+09, HBB+21] Past work in few-shot learning was part of our motivation to study transfer. [LST15] showed few-shot learning for generating handwritten characters with probabilistic program induction inline with human capabilities of few-shot learning on such a task. [FAL17] showed that trying to design a model to be ﬁne-tunable can improve few-shot performance. [BMR+20] used existing benchmarks to show that meaningful transfer/few- shot learning can occur in large models on tasks like SuperGLUE [WPN+19]. Another notable work that helped motivate our investigation into transfer was sim-to-real transfer training for solving a Rubik’s cube with a robot hand [OAA+19], a setting in which the ﬁne-tuning data is far more expensive than the pre-training data. Another approach for measuring generalization we’re interested in is the development of increasingly difﬁcult language benchmarks [HBB+21]. 5 Limitations 1) Models weren’t tuned for ﬁne-tuning or code. We leveraged hyperparameters that were tuned for training from scratch on natural language [KMH +20]. We did a handful of learning rate scans for ﬁne-tuning larger models on small dataset sizes and didn’t see any improvement with other learning rates. But our scans were not comprehensives. 2) Models weren’t tuned for small datasets. For small datasets, training ended before the warmup was ﬁnished, so the learning schedule could confound the results. 3) We only measured transfer when ﬁne-tuning on python. It’s unclear if we’d observe a power law ﬁt for a broad set of distribution pairs. 94) We only measured transfer between distributions in an unsupervised setting. It’s not clear to what degree the ﬁndings would generalize to a supervised or reinforcement learning setup. 5) We didn’t ﬁnd a good closed-form model for from-scratch results as was seen in [KMH+20], though we believe more careful tuning could have produced such a model in line with their results. If we had such results we expect we could generate a closed-form equation for overall performance for ﬁne-tuned models rather than rely on relative performance in our deﬁnition. 6) We only measured performance on transformers. 7) Equations 3.1 and 3.2 don’t handle zero-shot case unless we use an approximation (i.e. ﬁne-tuning on 1 character) for the zero-shot case. 8) We didn’t explore the ability to make sure measurements more cheaply, either in context or through KL divergence. 6 Discussion 6.1 Potential uniﬁed scaling law for ﬁne-tuning Using equation 1.5 from [KMH+20] we ﬁnd the following result for overall loss on a ﬁne-tuned model in the low-data regime: L≈ [(NC N )αN αD + DC k(DF)α(N)β ]αD (6.1) To generate equation 6.1 we have simply substituted effective data from transfer, DT, as given in equation 1.1 for the dataset size D in [KMH+20], which was ﬁt to language models trained from scratch. [SK20] attempts to explain the power-law from [KMH +20] as arising from neural networks performing regression on a data manifold of intrinsic dimensiond. Speculatively, we think the scaling laws of transfer ﬁt that picture, where pre-training tiles a portion of the downstream manifold at a lower density than training directly on the downstream task. 6.2 Speculative estimates for why large models would be few-shot learners The effective data multiplier goes down as we increase the size of the ﬁne-tuning dataset, DF. When we use equation 1.1 to extrapolate all the way down to approximately zero-shot, 1 character, we estimate that pre-trained models are equivalent to training from scratch on 3.7e8 characters of python when pre-trained on text with a model the size of GPT-3 [BMR +20]. If we increase this to a few-shot, say 300 characters, we multiply our effective data DE by a factor of 2.8. Given this analysis, it’s not surprising that few-shot scores on SuperGLUE [WPN+19] were 10-15 points higher than zero-shot scores [BMR +20]. The above analysis is relatively speculative because we extrapolated up in model size by two orders of magnitude and downwards in the amount of data by 5 orders of magnitude. We also equated data in context to data ﬁne-tuned on. Similar calculations for text + code pre-training give an estimate of DE = 4.1e9 characters, with 300 char- acters of examples worth a factor 1.7x. We were a bit surprised here, because our best guess before running these experiments would have been that making other programming languages half of the pre-training dataset would have increased few-shot transfer/effective data by more than 10x. One might have the concern that trace amounts of python in the text dataset could impact the transfer coefﬁcients for these experiments. We did additional experiments to mitigate this concern, which are described in Appendix F. 6.3 Potential applications of these scaling laws 1. If collecting more data is expensive the power-law form of transfer suggests a potentially useful and cheap experiment when trying to decide whether or not to collect more data to ﬁne-tune a pre- trained model on. One could ﬁne-tune a model with a 1% and 10% of the existing dataset. Next one could vary the model size given the full ﬁne-tuning dataset and estimate the lost performance in terms of a reduction in model size. We expect for many applications there will continue to be valuable, expensive to collect data, and that it will be useful to be able to make the decision as to whether to gather more such data in a principled way. One example of an expensive dataset is human preferences of what makes a good summary [SOW+20]. 102. It’s easier to generate simple equations for scaling laws where performance is measured in loss rather than accuracy for a downstream task[BMR+20]. Scaling laws posed in terms of effective data could provide an alternative, better behaved trend to compare architectures and algorithms. 6.4 Core factors vs details Previous work showed that the core factors affecting from-scratch performance included data, compute, and parameters [KMH+20, HKK+20]. They showed that performance only depended weakly on details like depth, width, and the number of attention heads. We believe ﬁne-tuned performance is likely similar, but where data is split into pre-trained and ﬁne-tuned data. For instance, we expect we’d observe smaller effects for tuning the hyperparameters for the ﬁne-tuning distribution, changing how many epochs we pre-train, and smoothly transitioning between the distributions than for changing the amount of ﬁne-tuning data or the pre-training distribution. We’d be excited to see future work evaluating this claim. 6.5 How similar are Python and English? We believe the dissimilarity of English and Python is representative of transfer between distant distributions that will be of interest in the future. There is English within python code (docstrings, comments, and function names). However, python is a “formal language” for communicating instructions to a computer and English is an informal language for communicating between people. We can imagine distributions that are further apart, for instance, English and Math. We can also think of distributions that feel relatively close, like English:French, Wikipedia:arxiv, and so on. Given the distance between distributions of future interest, we’d argue that transfer between text and code tells us something meaningful about transfer between distant distributions. 6.6 Ossiﬁcation Our small ﬁne-tuned models were unable to reach trained from scratch performance even as they were trained on 10x or 100x D(N), as shown in Figure 6. This is evidence for the intuition some hold that given inﬁnite data one is better off training entirely on distribution and suggests signiﬁcant pre-training might be impractical in terms of compute and tuning under such circumstances. This suggests that the weights can saturate or “ossify”, where they become unable to absorb new information well, and that ossiﬁcation scales predictably. That could be similar to saying that the prior learned in pre-training becomes counterproductive if it’s learned with too much relative strength. We may see an analogous phenomena in humans, where there seems to be a large advantage in being trained for a sport from a young age, thus avoiding the opportunity to develop bad habits. 6.7 Future work we’re particularly excited about 1. Measuring transfer coefﬁcients between more unsupervised distributions. 2. Measuring transfer coefﬁcient where the target distribution is much more general and/or a set of tasks. 3. Transfer scaling laws where the from-scratch comparisons are better behaved and can generate a uniﬁed predictive equation, such as 6.1. 4. Transfer scaling laws in supervised and reinforcement learning settings. 5. Transfer scaling laws comparing Transformers to other architectures. 6. A method to cheaply predict the ideal pre-training ratio for a pair of datasets A and B to maximize performance on a target distribution C, for which we have limited data. It’d be exciting if that ratio were a relatively simple function of the transfer coefﬁcients. 7. Given multiple target distributions/downstream tasks, each with limited amounts of data, a set of alpha measurements could potentially enable the construction of an optimal pre-training data split of whatever large datasets would be tractable to put together. 7 Conclusion We’ve shown that transfer is measurable within language models of a wide range of sizes and that it scales predictably. The units we measure transfer in, data, are intuitive, and given pre-trained models our approach 11can be used to take such measurements cheaply in the low data regime. We believe our approach is a novel and useful way to understand data as an ML ingredient and the generality of AI systems. We’ve generated scaling laws for ﬁne-tuning, which has recently become a subject of wide interest. These results help predict the performance, compute, and data needs for scaled-up ﬁne-tuned models. new_method.method:
Open Problems: Current sub-billion-parameter LLMs (e.g. 125 M–1 B) already run fast at inference but still require hundreds of GPU-days and >10¹⁹ FLOPs to pre-train on 0.5-1 T tokens. Existing acceleration methods (deep-thin design, tokenizer compression, staged growth, memory tricks) each save ≤25 % compute and usually trade-off either final quality (aggressive sharing) or implementation complexity (multigrid / pipeline). The key open problem is therefore:
How can we cut the end-to-end pre-training cost of tiny LLMs by ≥40 % *without* hurting downstream accuracy or increasing inference latency, using an architecture that stays PyTorch-friendly and hardware-agnostic?
Methods: We propose Progressive Layer-Activation & Distillation Transformer (PLAD-T), a two-phase training architecture that couples (A) weight-shared deep-thin transformers with (B) stage-wise layer activation and self-distillation.

1. Static network skeleton
   • 2L physical blocks are instantiated, where L≈32–48 for 125 M and L≈44–60 for 350 M/1 B.  
   • Every *pair* of adjacent blocks shares all weights (immediate weight sharing as in MobileLLM-LS) → parameter count unchanged, depth doubled logically.  
   • Blocks are reversible and use GQA + SwiGLU; projections are factorised (Q==K); vocab trimmed (48 k).

2. Phase-1 “Half-active” training (≈60 % of steps)
   • Only the odd blocks are active; even blocks are gated by an inexpensive identity switch.  
   • Compute ≈½; gradients only flow through active blocks.

3. Phase-2 progressive activation (remaining 40 %)  
   • Every K steps we un-gate a small batch of even blocks.  
   • When an even block is activated it is initialised by *self-distillation*: we copy the odd neighbour’s weights and attach a lightweight (rank-4) adapter that is trained with a KL loss to match the frozen teacher’s hidden states for 1 epoch.  
   • After adapter convergence, both blocks are jointly trained normally.

4. Auxiliary tricks (orthogonal to main idea)  
   • Sequence-length curriculum (128→2 k) like Li et al. 2021.  
   • Token-drop routing: first 70 % of training uses 50 % token keep-rate via confidence based pruning to further cut FLOPs.  
   • Training recipe: AdamW, LR scaled for smaller active depth, batch 2 M tokens.

Why it differs: Unlike staged-training (grow width/depth *and* parameters) or block-sharing (full cost from step-1), PLAD-T keeps total parameters constant while paying compute for only half the layers during most of training. Distillation at activation time preserves information therefore avoids the quality drop seen in immediate-sharing baselines.
Experimental Setup: Corpora  • Same 1 T multilingual tokens (PanGu / MobileLLM data) for fair comparison.

Models  • Baselines: MobileLLM-350 M, MobileLLM-LS-350 M, PanGu-π-1B-Pro, staged-training GPT-Base-390 M.  • Ours: PLAD-T-350 M, PLAD-T-1 B.

Compute budget  • Train all models on 32×A100 40 GB; log wall-clock, consumed GPU-hours & theoretical FLOPs.

Evaluation  • OpenCompass (MMLU, CMMLU, C-Eval, AGIEval), reasoning (BoolQ, PIQA), summarisation (XSum), chat (AlpacaEval, MT-Bench).  • Convergence curves (loss vs tokens).  • Inference latency & peak RAM – must match MobileLLM-LS.

Ablations  • Remove token-drop.  • Skip self-distillation.  • Vary Phase-1 portion (40/60/80 %).

Robustness  • Fine-tune on 3 downstream tasks with 1-5 % of data to ensure no forgetting.  • Quantisation to W8A8 to test hardware friendliness.
Result: We expect:
• PLAD-T reduces total training FLOPs by ~42 % and wall-clock by 30–35 % versus MobileLLM-LS, confirmed by profiler.  
• Final zero-shot average score on OpenCompass within ±0.3 of MobileLLM-LS (350 M) and +1.5 over non-shared MobileLLM, beating PanGu-π-1B on tokens-per-param efficiency.  
• Inference throughput identical to LS baseline; memory unchanged.  
• Ablation shows self-distillation recovers ≈2 pp accuracy lost by simple copy, and Phase-1 fraction correlates smoothly with compute/quality trade-off.  
• Quantised W8A8 version keeps <0.5 pp drop, showing compatibility.
Conclusion: PLAD-T demonstrates that *when* each parameter starts receiving gradient updates is as important as *how many* parameters a tiny LLM has. By activating only half of the network for most of training and seamlessly distilling knowledge into the rest later, we achieve large-scale compute savings without architectural overhead or inference cost. This bridges staged-growth and weight-sharing ideas, yielding a practical recipe that can be plugged into existing PyTorch/DeepSpeed code.

Practically, PLAD-T lowers the entry barrier for organisations training on-device class LLMs, cutting GPU bills by ~⅓. Academically, it opens avenues for schedule-aware network design and finer-grained progressive training (e.g., token-specific layer activation, curriculum on depth). Future work can combine PLAD-T with quantised training and mixture-of-experts to push compute efficiency even further.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
Title: Validating Progressive Layer-Activation & Distillation Transformer (PLAD-T)

Overview
We propose three complementary experiments that together verify: (1) end-to-end compute savings without accuracy loss, (2) necessity of self-distillation and the progressive schedule, and (3) hardware friendliness, unchanged inference cost, and quantization/fine-tuning robustness. All are implementable in Python with PyTorch/HuggingFace.

Common components
- Code base: PyTorch ≥2.1, HuggingFace Transformers/Datasets/Tokenizers, Accelerate or DeepSpeed optional.
- Datasets (scaled to fit budget):
  - Pretraining: SlimPajama-627B subset (e.g., 1–5B tokens), or FineWeb-edu small. Validation on The Pile val and WikiText-103.
  - Downstream eval: HellaSwag, PIQA, BoolQ (few-shot), and WikiText/PG19 perplexity.
- Models (scaled sanity setup):
  - Tiny-PLAD-T-60M and Tiny-PLAD-T-120M for resource-friendly runs; Larger PLAD-T-350M if GPUs allow.
  - Baselines: LS baseline (pairwise weight sharing active from step 1), Non-shared baseline (same param budget via narrower depth/width).
- Metrics:
  - Compute: wall-clock, GPU-hours, theoretical FLOPs (estimator), tokens/sec.
  - Quality: val cross-entropy vs tokens, final perplexity, zero-shot/few-shot accuracy.
  - Inference: latency, throughput, peak memory.

Experiment 1: End-to-end pretraining head-to-head (compute vs accuracy)
Goal
Show PLAD-T achieves ≥40% pretraining FLOPs savings and ~same or better final quality vs LS baseline while keeping inference cost identical.

Design
- Configs (example for 120M):
  - Vocabulary: 48k BPE; context length curriculum 128→1k.
  - Blocks: 24 logical pairs (48 logical layers). Each pair shares weights. GQA heads, SwiGLU MLP.
  - Phase 1: odd blocks active only (≈60% steps). Even blocks are identity gates.
  - Phase 2: progressively activate even blocks in batches of 2 pairs every K steps; upon activation, copy odd neighbor weights, attach rank-4 adapters; 1 epoch of distillation per activated batch, then merge adapters and continue joint training.
- Baselines trained with same tokens, optimizer, batch size, LR schedule.
  - LS baseline: identical architecture and weight sharing, but all layers active from step 1, no progressive gating.
  - Optional Non-shared baseline: same params, conventional depth with thinner width.
- Token-drop routing: Off for primary comparison; add as ablation in Exp2.

Procedure
1) Train PLAD-T and LS for N tokens (e.g., 1B) on 8×A100 or 4×A100; log profiler traces periodically to estimate FLOPs.
2) Track val loss vs tokens; early-stop both at same token budget.
3) After training, measure inference latency, throughput, peak RAM on A100 and a consumer GPU (e.g., 3090).
4) Evaluate zero/few-shot tasks and perplexity.

Success criteria
- ≥40% reduction in theoretical FLOPs and ≥25–35% wall-clock saving at equal tokens.
- Final perplexity within ±0.3 PPL or ±0.2 nats of LS, and comparable zero-shot accuracies.
- Inference latency/throughput/memory parity with LS.

Experiment 2: Ablations and schedule sensitivity
Goal
Demonstrate that self-distillation and the progressive schedule are necessary to preserve accuracy while saving compute; characterize compute/quality trade-offs.

Variants
- PLAD-T w/o self-distillation: activate even blocks by copying weights only; no adapters, no matching loss.
- PLAD-T with MSE vs KL: try L2/MSE on normalized hidden states vs KL on projected logits.
- Phase-1 fraction: 40%, 60%, 80%.
- Activation granularity: activate 1, 2, or 4 pairs per stage.
- Token-drop: on vs off (simple 50% keep-rate curriculum; reported for completeness even if compute impact is modest without kernel changes).

Measurements
- Final perplexity and eval accuracy after fixed tokens.
- Convergence speed (loss vs tokens) and recovery after each activation step.
- Representation similarity: SVCCA/CKA between teacher (odd) outputs and newly activated even-block outputs before/after distillation.
- Compute: wall-clock and theoretical FLOPs per variant.

Expected findings
- Self-distillation recovers ~1–2 pp accuracy compared to copy-only.
- Longer Phase-1 yields more compute savings but slight quality drop; smooth trade-off curve.
- MSE on hidden states is sufficient; KL on projected logits may give a small additional gain.

Experiment 3: Hardware friendliness, profiling, quantization, and fine-tuning robustness
Goal
Prove PLAD-T’s savings appear in real profilers, inference cost is unchanged, the model quantizes cleanly to W8A8, and fine-tunes normally.

Design
- Micro-bench: torch.profiler for forward+backward on representative batch sizes at three points: Phase-1 midpoint, just after an activation event, and final model; compare to LS.
- Inference: latency and throughput at batch sizes {1, 4, 16} and sequence lengths {256, 1k}.
- Quantization: dynamic W8A8 of Linear layers with torch.ao.quantization; measure eval drop and latency change.
- Fine-tuning: LoRA fine-tune on 1–5% of datasets (SST-2, AG News, BoolQ); compare PLAD-T vs LS improvements and stability.

Success criteria
- Profiler shows ~50% fewer layer kernels in Phase-1 and ~40% aggregate FLOPs saving over training.
- Inference metrics match LS (same weights, shared-pair layout; adapters merged).
- W8A8 drop <0.5 pp on downstream tasks; latency improves or stays similar.
- Fine-tuning reaches comparable or better accuracy within same steps.

Implementation sketch (minimal but runnable)
Note: This is a compact, self-contained skeleton showing: weight sharing by pairs, gating, progressive activation, low-rank adapters, distillation, adapter merge, FLOPs estimate, and profiling hooks. Replace the TinyBlock with a proper TransformerBlock (attention+MLP) for real runs.

Dependencies
- pip install torch torchvision torchaudio
- pip install transformers datasets accelerate

Code

import math, time, copy, itertools, contextlib
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Optional
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

# ----------------------- Core modules -----------------------
class SwiGLU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.w1 = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)
        self.w2 = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff, bias=False)
        self.w3 = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.w3(F.silu(self.w1(x)) * self.w2(x))

class MHAGQA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, n_kv_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.n_kv_heads = n_kv_heads
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
        # Factorized projections: share Q and K sizes, allow GQA
        self.Wq = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.Wk = nn.Linear(d_model, self.head_dim * n_kv_heads, bias=False)
        self.Wv = nn.Linear(d_model, self.head_dim * n_kv_heads, bias=False)
        self.Wo = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x, attn_mask=None):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.Wq(x).view(B, T, self.n_heads, C // self.n_heads).transpose(1,2)
        kv = self.Wk(x), self.Wv(x)
        k = kv[0].view(B, T, self.n_kv_heads, C // self.n_heads).transpose(1,2)
        v = kv[1].view(B, T, self.n_kv_heads, C // self.n_heads).transpose(1,2)
        # broadcast kv across query heads
        if self.n_kv_heads == 1:
            k = k.expand(B, self.n_heads, T, k.size(-1))
            v = v.expand(B, self.n_heads, T, v.size(-1))
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-1,-2)) / math.sqrt(k.size(-1))
        if attn_mask is not None:
            att = att + attn_mask  # additive mask
        p = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        y = (p @ v).transpose(1,2).contiguous().view(B, T, C)
        return self.Wo(y)

class LayerNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d):
        super().__init__()
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(d))
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d))
    def forward(self, x, eps=1e-5):
        mu = x.mean(-1, keepdim=True)
        var = (x - mu).pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True)
        xhat = (x - mu) / torch.sqrt(var + eps)
        return xhat * self.weight + self.bias

class TinyBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, n_kv_heads, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1 = LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attn = MHAGQA(d_model, n_heads, n_kv_heads)
        self.ln2 = LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.mlp = SwiGLU(d_model, d_ff)
    def forward(self, x, attn_mask=None):
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x), attn_mask)
        x = x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))
        return x

# Low-rank adapter (LoRA-style) that can be merged into Linear
class LoRAAdapter(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, linear: nn.Linear, rank=4, alpha=1.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = linear
        self.rank = rank
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(linear.out_features, rank))
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(rank, linear.in_features))
        nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.B, a=math.sqrt(5))
        self.scaling = alpha / rank
        self.merged = False
    def forward(self, x):
        base = self.linear(x)
        update = F.linear(x, self.B)  # [*, r]
        update = F.linear(update, self.A) * self.scaling
        return base + update
    def merge(self):
        if self.merged: return
        with torch.no_grad():
            W = self.linear.weight
            delta = (self.A @ self.B) * self.scaling
            self.linear.weight.copy_(W + delta)
        self.merged = True
    def disable_update(self):
        # freeze adapter weights for inference if not merged
        for p in [self.A, self.B]: p.requires_grad_(False)

# Wrap a TinyBlock with optional adapters on its Linear layers
class AdaptedBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base_block: TinyBlock, rank=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base_block
        # Replace linear layers with adapter-wrapped versions
        self.base.attn.Wq = LoRAAdapter(self.base.attn.Wq, rank)
        self.base.attn.Wk = LoRAAdapter(self.base.attn.Wk, rank)
        self.base.attn.Wv = LoRAAdapter(self.base.attn.Wv, rank)
        self.base.attn.Wo = LoRAAdapter(self.base.attn.Wo, rank)
        self.base.mlp.w1 = LoRAAdapter(self.base.mlp.w1, rank)
        self.base.mlp.w2 = LoRAAdapter(self.base.mlp.w2, rank)
        self.base.mlp.w3 = LoRAAdapter(self.base.mlp.w3, rank)
    def forward(self, x, attn_mask=None):
        return self.base(x, attn_mask)
    def merge_all(self):
        for mod in [self.base.attn.Wq, self.base.attn.Wk, self.base.attn.Wv, self.base.attn.Wo, self.base.mlp.w1, self.base.mlp.w2, self.base.mlp.w3]:
            mod.merge()

@dataclass
class PLADConfig:
    d_model: int = 512
    n_heads: int = 8
    n_kv_heads: int = 1
    d_ff: int = 1536
    n_pairs: int = 12  # total logical depth is 2 * n_pairs
    vocab_size: int = 48000
    max_seq: int = 1024

class PLADTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cfg: PLADConfig):
        super().__init__()
        self.cfg = cfg
        self.embed = nn.Embedding(cfg.vocab_size, cfg.d_model)
        self.blocks_odd: List[TinyBlock] = nn.ModuleList()
        self.blocks_even: List[nn.Module] = nn.ModuleList()  # either identity, shared pointer, or adapted
        for i in range(cfg.n_pairs):
            odd = TinyBlock(cfg.d_model, cfg.n_heads, cfg.n_kv_heads, cfg.d_ff)
            self.blocks_odd.append(odd)
            # even starts as identity gate (inactive)
            self.blocks_even.append(nn.Identity())
        self.ln_f = LayerNorm(cfg.d_model)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(cfg.d_model, cfg.vocab_size, bias=False)
        # share weights within pairs: even is pointer to odd by default when activated
    def forward(self, idx, attn_mask=None):
        x = self.embed(idx)
        for odd, even in zip(self.blocks_odd, self.blocks_even):
            x = odd(x, attn_mask)
            x = even(x, attn_mask)  # Identity or shared/adapted block
        x = self.ln_f(x)
        logits = self.lm_head(x)
        return logits

# Progressive activation utilities
class Activator:
    def __init__(self, model: PLADTransformer, rank=4):
        self.m = model
        self.rank = rank
    def is_active(self, pair_idx):
        return not isinstance(self.m.blocks_even[pair_idx], nn.Identity)
    def activate_pair(self, pair_idx, use_adapters=True):
        if self.is_active(pair_idx):
            return
        # Copy odd weights to a new even block that shares parameters or uses adapters
        odd = self.m.blocks_odd[pair_idx]
        even_base = copy.deepcopy(odd)
        if use_adapters:
            even = AdaptedBlock(even_base, rank=self.rank)
        else:
            even = even_base
        # Weight sharing pointer: to mimic LS baseline, we can set even to odd
        # For PLAD-T, we want a distinct module initialized from odd (copied), then trained jointly
        self.m.blocks_even[pair_idx] = even
    def merge_adapters(self):
        for i in range(self.m.cfg.n_pairs):
            even = self.m.blocks_even[i]
            if isinstance(even, AdaptedBlock):
                even.merge_all()

# Distillation step: match normalized hidden states (MSE) of teacher (odd output) and student (even output)
@torch.no_grad()
def get_post_odd_hidden(model: PLADTransformer, x, attn_mask, pair_idx):
    h = model.embed(x)
    for i in range(pair_idx+1):
        h = model.blocks_odd[i](h, attn_mask)
        if i < pair_idx:
            # pass through even (identity or active) to reach next odd
            h = model.blocks_even[i](h, attn_mask)
    return h

def distill_even_block(model: PLADTransformer, pair_idx, data_iter, steps=500, lr=5e-4, device="cuda"):
    model.train()
    odd_teacher = copy.deepcopy(model.blocks_odd[pair_idx]).to(device).eval()
    for p in odd_teacher.parameters(): p.requires_grad_(False)
    even_module = model.blocks_even[pair_idx]
    assert not isinstance(even_module, nn.Identity), "Even block must be active to distill"
    # Optimize only adapter params if present, else all params of even block
    params = [p for p in even_module.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=lr, betas=(0.9,0.95), weight_decay=0.01)
    for t in range(steps):
        batch = next(data_iter)
        x = batch["input_ids"].to(device)
        attn_mask = None
        with torch.no_grad():
            h_teacher = odd_teacher(get_post_odd_hidden(model, x, attn_mask, pair_idx-1) if pair_idx>0 else model.embed(x), attn_mask)
        h_student_in = get_post_odd_hidden(model, x, attn_mask, pair_idx-1) if pair_idx>0 else model.embed(x)
        h_student = even_module(h_student_in, attn_mask)
        # Normalize and compute MSE
        ht = F.layer_norm(h_teacher, normalized_shape=(h_teacher.size(-1),))
        hs = F.layer_norm(h_student, normalized_shape=(h_student.size(-1),))
        loss = F.mse_loss(hs, ht)
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

# FLOPs estimator (approx): Transformer layer cost per token ~ 2*d_model^2 + 4*d_model*d_ff + attention term

def estimate_flops_per_token(cfg: PLADConfig, seq_len: int, active_pairs: int):
    d = cfg.d_model
    dff = cfg.d_ff
    H = cfg.n_heads
    layers = active_pairs * 2  # odd+even
    attn = 2*d*d + 2*seq_len*d*d/H  # rough
    mlp = 4*d*dff + 2*dff*d
    per_layer = attn + mlp
    return layers * per_layer

# ----------------------- Training loop sketch -----------------------

def train_plad(model, tokenizer, dataset, total_steps=20000, phase1_frac=0.6, activate_every=2000, device="cuda"):
    model.to(device)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95), weight_decay=0.1)
    activator = Activator(model, rank=4)
    dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=8, shuffle=True, drop_last=True)
    data_iter = iter(itertools.cycle(dl))
    phase1_steps = int(total_steps * phase1_frac)
    next_activation = phase1_steps
    pairs_to_activate = list(range(model.cfg.n_pairs))
    activated_idx = 0
    for step in range(total_steps):
        batch = next(data_iter)
        x = batch["input_ids"].to(device)
        logits = model(x)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[:, :-1, :].contiguous().view(-1, logits.size(-1)), x[:, 1:].contiguous().view(-1))
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        # Progressive activation schedule
        if step == next_activation and activated_idx < len(pairs_to_activate):
            # Activate 2 pairs per stage as example
            for _ in range(2):
                if activated_idx >= len(pairs_to_activate): break
                pidx = pairs_to_activate[activated_idx]
                activator.activate_pair(pidx, use_adapters=True)
                # Short distillation epoch for the new even block
                distill_even_block(model, pidx, data_iter, steps=300, lr=5e-4, device=device)
                activated_idx += 1
            next_activation += activate_every
    # Merge adapters for inference
    activator.merge_adapters()
    return model

# ----------------------- Baseline LS training -----------------------

def make_ls_baseline(cfg: PLADConfig):
    m = PLADTransformer(cfg)
    # Immediately activate all even blocks by sharing weights (pointer to odd)
    for i in range(cfg.n_pairs):
        # share by reference: both odd and even point to same module
        m.blocks_even[i] = m.blocks_odd[i]  # weight sharing
    return m

# ----------------------- Data prep (example) -----------------------
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

def build_tiny_text_dataset(tokenizer_name="gpt2", max_len=256, n_samples=100000):
    tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(tokenizer_name)
    tok.model_max_length = max_len
    raw = load_dataset("wikitext", "wikitext-2-raw-v1", split="train")
    def tok_map(ex):
        ids = tok(ex["text"], truncation=True, max_length=max_len, return_tensors=None)["input_ids"]
        return {"input_ids": ids}
    ds = raw.map(tok_map, remove_columns=raw.column_names)
    ds = ds.select(range(min(n_samples, len(ds))))
    ds.set_format(type="torch")
    return ds, tok

# ----------------------- Profiling utilities -----------------------
@contextlib.contextmanager
def cuda_timer():
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); start = time.time()
    yield
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); end = time.time()
    print(f"Elapsed: {end-start:.3f}s")

# Example usage (toy)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    cfg = PLADConfig(d_model=384, n_heads=6, n_kv_heads=1, d_ff=1536, n_pairs=6, vocab_size=50257, max_seq=256)
    ds, tok = build_tiny_text_dataset(max_len=cfg.max_seq, n_samples=5000)
    plad = PLADTransformer(cfg)
    with cuda_timer():
        plad = train_plad(plad, tok, ds, total_steps=1000, phase1_frac=0.6, activate_every=200)
    # LS baseline
    ls = make_ls_baseline(cfg)
    # Train LS briefly for comparison (same steps; omitted here for brevity)

# ----------------------- Quantization (dynamic W8A8) -----------------------
# After training and merging adapters:
# torch.ao.quantization dynamic example on Linear layers

def dynamic_w8a8(model: nn.Module):
    qconfig = torch.ao.quantization.qconfig.default_dynamic_qconfig
    to_quantize = {nn.Linear}
    mp = torch.ao.quantization.quantize_dynamic(model, to_quantize, dtype=torch.qint8)
    return mp

# ----------------------- Inference benchmark -----------------------

def benchmark_inference(model, seq_len=256, batch=1, device="cuda"):
    model.eval().to(device)
    x = torch.randint(0, model.cfg.vocab_size, (batch, seq_len), device=device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        torch.cuda.synchronize(); t0=time.time()
        for _ in range(50):
            _= model(x)
        torch.cuda.synchronize(); dt=time.time()-t0
    print(f"Throughput tokens/s: {batch*seq_len*50/dt:.0f}")

Practical notes
- For real experiments, replace TinyBlock with a production-grade Transformer block (flash-attn kernels, rotary embeddings, causal mask, dropout). The gating and adapter logic remains identical.
- Use Accelerate/DeepSpeed ZeRO for memory scaling. Checkpoints: save activation stage metadata.
- Token-drop routing (optional): implement a curriculum by sub-sampling tokens for loss and using sequence packing to realize some compute savings; leave off in primary runs to isolate PLAD-T effects.
- Logging: use WandB to track loss vs tokens, FLOPs estimates, activation events, and CKA metrics.

Readouts to include in the paper/report
- Plot loss vs tokens for PLAD-T vs LS.
- Bar chart of GPU-hours and theoretical FLOPs.
- Inference latency table (BS: 1/4/16; SL: 256/1k).
- Ablation table: copy-only vs distilled; phase-1 fractions; activation batch size.
- CKA alignment before/after distillation.

Resource estimates (indicative)
- Tiny-120M on 1B tokens, seq 512, batch 1M tokens/step: 4×A100 40GB for ~2–3 days (LS), PLAD-T ~30% faster wall-clock.
- The provided toy code runs on a single GPU for sanity checks; scale up configs for full results.

Risk and mitigations
- If distillation stalls: increase adapter rank to 8 or extend steps by 1.5×.
- If quality gap emerges at the end: shorten Phase-1 to 50% and increase activation frequency.
- Ensure adapter merge before inference to avoid latency penalties.

These three experiments, with the included code skeleton, allow rigorous validation of PLAD-T’s compute savings, accuracy parity, and hardware friendliness in a PyTorch-friendly, hardware-agnostic manner.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
Title: Validating Progressive Layer-Activation & Distillation Transformer (PLAD-T)

This specification expands each item in the Experiment Strategy with concrete, reproducible details, PyTorch-first implementations, code examples, metrics, and reliability safeguards. It integrates related verification items to minimize redundant runs while keeping results isolatable.

----------------------------------------
Common components (applies to all experiments)
----------------------------------------
- Code base and key libraries
  - Python ≥ 3.10, PyTorch ≥ 2.1, CUDA 11.8+ (or ROCm if AMD)
  - HuggingFace Transformers (≥ 4.41), Datasets, Tokenizers
  - Accelerate (for multi-GPU) or DeepSpeed (ZeRO-2/3 optional)
  - PEFT (LoRA adapters), bitsandbytes (optional int8 on GPU), torch.ao.quantization (dynamic W8A8)
  - flash-attn (optional) for efficient attention kernels; torch.compile for fusion
  - Weights & Biases or MLflow for logging; einops; tqdm
  - Evaluation: lm-eval-harness (HellaSwag, PIQA, BoolQ); perplexity on WikiText, PG19
  - Representation similarity: torch-cka (pip install torch-cka) or cca-zoo (for SVCCA)

- Datasets
  - Pretraining: SlimPajama-627B or FineWeb-edu. For compute-feasible validation: use a 1–5B token slice. Maintain a fixed, shuffled index mapping for all runs to ensure identical sample ordering across baselines and ablations.
  - Validation: The Pile val split, WikiText-103, a 10M token held-out from the pretraining mixture.
  - Downstream: HellaSwag, PIQA, BoolQ from lm-eval; perplexity on WikiText/PG19; optional summarization XSum for ablation subset.

- Tokenization
  - 48k BPE (SentencePiece) for parity with method; if unavailable, use LLaMA tokenizer (32k) for sanity runs and document deviation.

- Models
  - Tiny-PLAD-T-60M and -120M (sanity/ablation), PLAD-T-350M (scaling run if budget allows).
  - Baselines: LS baseline (pairwise immediate weight-sharing, all layers active from step 1); Non-shared baseline (same parameter budget, adjusted width/depth without pairwise sharing).

- Training recipe (shared unless noted)
  - Optimizer: AdamW (betas 0.9/0.95, weight decay 0.1); grad clipping 1.0
  - LR: cosine decay with warmup 1–3% of steps; peak LR tuned per model size (e.g., 3e-4 for 60M/120M; 2e-4 for 350M)
  - Batch size target: 1–2M tokens per update via gradient accumulation; use sequence packing to minimize padding
  - Sequence-length curriculum: 128 → 256 → 512 → 1k (or 2k for larger) over fixed token milestones
  - Regularization: dropout 0–0.1 as needed; attention dropout 0–0.1; weight decay as above
  - Mixed precision: bfloat16 preferred; fallback FP16 with loss scaling
  - Checkpointing: save every 0.5–1% of tokens; activation stage metadata included

- Reliability and fairness controls
  - Three seeds per main condition (0/1/2); report mean ± std; use paired statistical tests where applicable
  - Identical data order, augmentation, and optimizer schedules across compared runs
  - Early stop disabled for head-to-head; train to pre-specified token budget
  - Log: tokens seen, steps, learning rate, grad norms, FLOPs estimates, wall-clock, GPU utilization, memory, activation events

- FLOPs and throughput accounting
  - Theoretical FLOPs per token per layer using standard transformer estimates (attention + MLP); account for active-layer count per step
  - Realized wall-clock GPU-hours from cluster scheduler logs; per-step tokens/sec via moving average; torch.profiler FLOPs samples at scheduled intervals

- Inference benchmarking
  - Latency (p50/p95) and throughput for batch sizes {1, 4, 16} and seq lengths {256, 1k, 2k}; peak memory; measure on A100-40GB and one consumer GPU (e.g., 3090 or A6000)

- Quantization
  - Primary: torch.ao.quantization dynamic int8 for Linear layers (W8A8 on CPU); optional GPU int8 via bitsandbytes LLM.int8 and SmoothQuant (optimum/intel-neural-compressor) when available

- Reproducibility
  - Publish config files and run scripts; freeze library versions; record environment; deterministic ops where feasible (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) with awareness of perf cost)


-------------------------------------------------------
Experiment 1: End-to-end pretraining head-to-head
-------------------------------------------------------
Goal
- Demonstrate ≥40% theoretical pretraining FLOPs reduction and 25–35% wall-clock saving versus LS baseline at equal token budget, with final accuracy within tolerance and identical inference cost.

Model configurations
- Tiny-PLAD-T-120M (recommended default for feasibility)
  - d_model: 640; n_heads: 8; n_kv_heads: 2 (GQA); d_ff: 4×d_model with SwiGLU (e.g., 2560); vocab: 48k; rotary embeddings; RMSNorm/LN
  - n_pairs: 12 → 24 logical layers; pairwise sharing (odd/even in a pair share initial weights when even is activated)
- Tiny-PLAD-T-60M (optional for faster iterations)
  - d_model: 512; n_heads: 8; n_kv_heads: 1; d_ff: 2048; n_pairs: 8 → 16 logical layers
- PLAD-T-350M (scaling)
  - d_model: 1024; n_heads: 16; n_kv_heads: 4; d_ff: 4096; n_pairs: 22 → 44 logical layers

PLAD-T training schedule
- Phase 1 (60% tokens): only odd blocks active; even blocks are identity gates; gradients flow only through active blocks
- Phase 2 (40% tokens): progressively un-gate even blocks in batches of B pairs every K steps (default B=2). When activating a pair i:
  - Initialize even block by copying odd block’s weights
  - Attach PEFT-LoRA adapters (rank r=4, alpha=8) to Linear layers of the even block only
  - Run a lightweight self-distillation sub-epoch: minimize MSE on normalized hidden states (or KL on a small projection head) between teacher (odd block frozen snapshot) and student (even block with adapters) for E steps (e.g., 1–2k mini-batch steps over a 50–100k token buffer)
  - Merge adapters into even block and continue joint training with both blocks trainable

Baselines (trained identically except activation)
- LS baseline: same skeleton, all even blocks active from step 1, sharing parameters with odd via a single module reference or hard weight tying; no gating or distillation
- Non-shared baseline: same parameter budget by reducing width/increasing depth appropriately; standard transformer (no pairwise sharing)

Compute expectation (closed-form)
- Let L be pairs, so logical depth is 2L. Baseline LS uses 2L active layers across all tokens
- PLAD-T compute (ignoring small distillation overhead):
  - Phase 1 (fraction f=0.6): L active layers → f×(L/(2L)) = 0.6×0.5 = 0.30 baseline equivalent
  - Phase 2 (1−f=0.4): active depth increases from L to 2L; average 1.5L → 0.4×(1.5L / 2L) = 0.4×0.75 = 0.30
  - Total ≈ 0.60 baseline equivalent; expected ~40% theoretical FLOPs reduction. Distillation sub-epochs add ~1–3% overhead, still ≥37% savings

Procedure
1) Initialize tokenizer and datasets; build a fixed shuffled index for reproducibility. Prepare dataloaders with sequence packing; set up curriculum schedule
2) Train PLAD-T and LS for the same token budget (e.g., 1B tokens for 120M; 250M for 60M pilot), 3 seeds each
3) Log theoretical FLOPs per step based on active layer count and sequence length; collect wall-clock and profiler samples every ~1% tokens
4) Post-training, merge all adapters; serialize model
5) Inference benchmarks on A100 and a consumer GPU; record latency, throughput, and peak memory; confirm parity with LS
6) Evaluate zero-/few-shot tasks (lm-eval-harness) and perplexity

Success criteria
- ≥40% theoretical FLOPs reduction; ≥25–35% wall-clock savings
- Validation CE within ±0.2 nats or perplexity within ±0.3 absolute; lm-eval scores within ±1 pp; no consistent degradation across seeds
- Inference latency/throughput/memory parity with LS (within noise)

Example code: PLAD-T with HuggingFace blocks, gating, progressive activation, PEFT-LoRA distillation

Note: This is a realistic skeleton that reuses HF modules. Replace the demo transformer class with Llama-like blocks when running large experiments. The gating and activation logic will remain identical.

```python
# pip install transformers datasets accelerate peft torch-cka bitsandbytes wandb
import math, copy, time, random
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Optional, Dict

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoTokenizer, PreTrainedModel
from transformers.models.llama.modeling_llama import (
    LlamaConfig, LlamaModel, LlamaForCausalLM, LlamaDecoderLayer
)
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, TaskType

# --------------- Utility: pairwise sharing & gating ---------------
@dataclass
class PLADRuntimeCfg:
    n_pairs: int
    phase1_frac: float = 0.6
    activate_batch_size: int = 2    # number of pairs to activate per stage
    distill_steps_per_pair: int = 1000
    lora_rank: int = 4
    lora_alpha: int = 8
    use_mse_hidden: bool = True

class GatedDecoder(nn.Module):
    """Wraps a list of HF decoder layers with odd-even pairs and runtime gating."""
    def __init__(self, base_layers: nn.ModuleList, n_pairs: int):
        super().__init__()
        assert len(base_layers) >= n_pairs, "Provide at least n_pairs layers for odd blocks"
        self.odd_layers = nn.ModuleList([base_layers[i] for i in range(n_pairs)])
        self.even_layers = nn.ModuleList([nn.Identity() for _ in range(n_pairs)])

    def forward(self, hidden_states, attention_mask=None, position_ids=None, **kwargs):
        for odd, even in zip(self.odd_layers, self.even_layers):
            hidden_states = odd(hidden_states, attention_mask=attention_mask, position_ids=position_ids, **kwargs)[0]
            # even may be Identity or a decoder layer
            if isinstance(even, nn.Identity):
                continue
            hidden_states = even(hidden_states, attention_mask=attention_mask, position_ids=position_ids, **kwargs)[0]
        return hidden_states

class PLADForCausalLM(PreTrainedModel):
    config_class = LlamaConfig
    def __init__(self, config: LlamaConfig, n_pairs: int):
        super().__init__(config)
        self.model = LlamaModel(config)
        # Replace decoder.layers with gated odd/even structure
        # Reuse first n_pairs layers for odd; start with even as Identity
        self.model.layers = GatedDecoder(self.model.layers, n_pairs)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(config.hidden_size, config.vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.post_init()

    def forward(self, input_ids=None, attention_mask=None, labels=None, **kwargs):
        out = self.model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, **kwargs)
        hidden_states = out  # already last hidden from GatedDecoder
        logits = self.lm_head(hidden_states)
        loss = None
        if labels is not None:
            shift_logits = logits[:, :-1].contiguous()
            shift_labels = labels[:, 1:].contiguous()
            loss = F.cross_entropy(shift_logits.view(-1, shift_logits.size(-1)), shift_labels.view(-1))
        return {'loss': loss, 'logits': logits}

class Activator:
    def __init__(self, model: PLADForCausalLM, runtime_cfg: PLADRuntimeCfg):
        self.m = model
        self.cfg = runtime_cfg
        self.n_pairs = runtime_cfg.n_pairs

    def is_active(self, idx):
        return not isinstance(self.m.model.layers.even_layers[idx], nn.Identity)

    def activate_pair_with_lora(self, idx):
        if self.is_active(idx):
            return
        # create even layer by deep-copying the odd layer weights
        odd: LlamaDecoderLayer = self.m.model.layers.odd_layers[idx]
        even: LlamaDecoderLayer = copy.deepcopy(odd)
        # attach LoRA adapters to Linear modules in attention and MLP
        peft_cfg = LoraConfig(
            task_type=TaskType.CAUSAL_LM,
            r=self.cfg.lora_rank,
            lora_alpha=self.cfg.lora_alpha,
            lora_dropout=0.0,
            target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
        )
        even = get_peft_model(even, peft_cfg)
        self.m.model.layers.even_layers[idx] = even

    @torch.no_grad()
    def merge_pair_lora(self, idx):
        even = self.m.model.layers.even_layers[idx]
        if hasattr(even, "merge_and_unload"):
            even.merge_and_unload()

# Hidden-state self-distillation for one pair
@torch.no_grad()
def _get_post_odd_hidden(m: PLADForCausalLM, input_ids, attention_mask, pair_idx):
    h = m.model.embed_tokens(input_ids) * (m.model.config.hidden_size ** 0.5)
    # rotary, positions etc. are handled inside layer; but for approximation we feed via layers
    for i in range(pair_idx + 1):
        h = m.model.layers.odd_layers[i](h, attention_mask=attention_mask)[0]
        if i < pair_idx:
            even = m.model.layers.even_layers[i]
            if not isinstance(even, nn.Identity):
                h = even(h, attention_mask=attention_mask)[0]
    return h

def distill_even_pair(model: PLADForCausalLM, pair_idx: int, data_iter, steps: int, device="cuda"):
    model.train()
    odd_teacher = copy.deepcopy(model.model.layers.odd_layers[pair_idx]).to(device).eval()
    for p in odd_teacher.parameters(): p.requires_grad_(False)
    even = model.model.layers.even_layers[pair_idx]
    # optimize only LoRA params if present; else all params of even block
    params = [p for n,p in even.named_parameters() if p.requires_grad]
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=5e-4, betas=(0.9,0.95), weight_decay=0.01)
    for t in range(steps):
        batch = next(data_iter)
        x = batch["input_ids"].to(device)
        attn = batch.get("attention_mask", (x != model.config.pad_token_id).long()).to(device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            teacher_in = _get_post_odd_hidden(model, x, attn, pair_idx-1) if pair_idx>0 else model.model.embed_tokens(x)
            h_teacher = odd_teacher(teacher_in, attention_mask=attn)[0]
        student_in = _get_post_odd_hidden(model, x, attn, pair_idx-1) if pair_idx>0 else model.model.embed_tokens(x)
        h_student = even(student_in, attention_mask=attn)[0]
        # normalize and MSE
        ht = F.layer_norm(h_teacher, (h_teacher.size(-1),))
        hs = F.layer_norm(h_student, (h_student.size(-1),))
        loss = F.mse_loss(hs, ht)
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

# Training loop with progressive activation
from itertools import cycle

def train_plad(
    model: PLADForCausalLM, 
    train_ds, 
    total_steps=20000, 
    runtime_cfg=PLADRuntimeCfg(n_pairs=12),
    batch_size=8,
    device="cuda",
):
    model.to(device)
    activator = Activator(model, runtime_cfg)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9,0.95), weight_decay=0.1)
    dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True, drop_last=True)
    data_iter = cycle(dl)

    phase1_steps = int(total_steps * runtime_cfg.phase1_frac)
    next_activation_step = phase1_steps
    pair_order = list(range(runtime_cfg.n_pairs))

    for step in range(total_steps):
        batch = next(data_iter)
        x = batch["input_ids"].to(device)
        attn = batch.get("attention_mask")
        out = model(input_ids=x, attention_mask=attn, labels=x)
        loss = out['loss']
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()

        # progressive activation
        if step == next_activation_step and len(pair_order) > 0:
            for _ in range(runtime_cfg.activate_batch_size):
                if not pair_order: break
                pidx = pair_order.pop(0)
                activator.activate_pair_with_lora(pidx)
                distill_even_pair(model, pidx, data_iter, steps=runtime_cfg.distill_steps_per_pair, device=device)
            next_activation_step += max(1, (total_steps - phase1_steps) // max(1, (runtime_cfg.n_pairs // runtime_cfg.activate_batch_size)))

    # merge adapters
    for i in range(runtime_cfg.n_pairs):
        activator.merge_pair_lora(i)
    return model
```

FLOPs estimator and logging hook

```python
def estimate_flops_per_token(d_model, d_ff, n_heads, seq_len, active_layers):
    # rough estimate per layer per token (forward+backward ~ 2x forward)
    # linear projections: ~ 2*d_model^2; MLP: ~ 8*d_model*d_ff; attention matmul: ~ 2*seq_len*(d_model^2/n_heads)
    attn = 2 * d_model * d_model + 2 * seq_len * (d_model * d_model // n_heads)
    mlp = 8 * d_model * d_ff
    per_layer_fwd = attn + mlp
    return active_layers * per_layer_fwd * 2  # account for backward

class FlopsLogger:
    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff, n_heads, seq_len):
        self.d_model, self.d_ff, self.n_heads, self.seq_len = d_model, d_ff, n_heads, seq_len
        self.accum = 0
    def step(self, active_layers, batch_tokens):
        flops_tok = estimate_flops_per_token(self.d_model, self.d_ff, self.n_heads, self.seq_len, active_layers)
        self.accum += flops_tok * batch_tokens
    def total(self):
        return self.accum
```

Experiment 2: Ablations and schedule sensitivity
------------------------------------------------------
Goal
- Establish necessity of self-distillation and progressive schedule; map compute/quality trade-offs.

Variants (each trained to the same token budget; try 2 seeds for grid, 3 seeds for key points)
- Distillation:
  1) Copy-only: activate even blocks by cloning odd weights; no adapters, no distillation
  2) MSE on normalized hidden states (default)
  3) KL on projected logits: learn a small projection head W: d→d to produce pseudo-logits and match teacher with KLDivLoss(log-softmax)
  4) Adapter rank sweep: LoRA rank r ∈ {0 (copy-only), 2, 4, 8}
- Phase 1 fraction f ∈ {0.4, 0.6, 0.8}
- Activation granularity B ∈ {1, 2, 4} pairs per stage
- Token-drop routing: off vs on (50% keep-rate for first 70% tokens; loss computed only on kept tokens; pack kept spans to reduce effective seq length during backward)

Measurements
- Convergence curves (val CE vs tokens) with vertical markers at activation events
- Final perplexity and lm-eval scores; compute estimates and wall-clock
- Recovery time after activation events (steps to regain pre-activation CE)
- Representation similarity: CKA/SVCCA between teacher odd and newly activated even outputs before and after distillation

CKA measurement example

```python
# pip install torch-cka
from torch_ckA import CKA

def cka_between_blocks(model, pair_idx, data_loader, device="cuda"):
    odd = model.model.layers.odd_layers[pair_idx]
    even = model.model.layers.even_layers[pair_idx]
    odd.eval(); even.eval()
    feats_odd, feats_even = [], []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for i, batch in enumerate(data_loader):
            if i>=10: break
            x = batch["input_ids"].to(device)
            attn = batch.get("attention_mask")
            h_in = _get_post_odd_hidden(model, x, attn, pair_idx-1) if pair_idx>0 else model.model.embed_tokens(x)
            feats_odd.append(odd(h_in, attention_mask=attn)[0].flatten(0,1).cpu())
            feats_even.append(even(h_in, attention_mask=attn)[0].flatten(0,1).cpu())
    X = torch.cat(feats_odd)
    Y = torch.cat(feats_even)
    cka = CKA(num_layers=1, device="cpu")
    return cka.linear_CKA(X, Y).item()
```

Expected findings
- Copy-only degrades final accuracy by ~1–2 pp; MSE recovers most; KL may add a slight gain in some setups
- f=0.8 yields larger savings but modest quality drop; smooth trade-off enables tuning to budget
- B=2 often balances stability and speed; B=4 risks larger loss spikes; B=1 smoother but slower
- Token-drop provides extra small savings when implemented with sequence packing for backprop; impact on quality negligible if keep-rate curriculum ramps back to 1.0

Integrated run plan to minimize overlap
- Use a shared set of base checkpoints at f=0.6, B=2. Branch to: copy-only, MSE, KL, r-sweep by resuming at the first activation event and replaying activation/distillation with different settings (saves 60% of initial compute)

----------------------------------------
Implementation details and safeguards
----------------------------------------
- Identity gating cost
  - Use nn.Identity for even blocks during Phase 1. This adds negligible overhead but preserves layer indexing simplicity and optimizer state consistency

- Weight sharing vs copying
  - LS baseline uses module aliasing (even points to odd) to ensure true weight sharing and identical inference cost
  - PLAD-T copies odd weights into even when activating; after adapters merge, odd and even are distinct, keeping total parameter count equal to LS (since LS shares within pair at inference as well). To match inference cost to LS, ensure the final number of computational layers and tensor shapes remain identical. Adapter parameters are merged into base weights and discarded

- Self-distillation stability
  - If distillation loss stalls: increase LoRA rank to 8, extend steps by 1.5×, or blend a small language modeling loss (e.g., 0.1× CE) during the distill sub-epoch

- Token-drop routing (optional)
  - Implement by masking the loss for a random subset of tokens guided by confidence (e.g., p(max)>τ). To realize compute savings, pack kept tokens into shorter contiguous spans for backprop—this reduces backward compute even if forward attention cost remains comparable. Keep this feature off for main comparisons to isolate PLAD-T effects, and evaluate separately in ablation

- Multi-GPU scaling
  - Use Accelerate/DeepSpeed ZeRO-2/3; enable gradient checkpointing to control activation memory. With flash-attn and torch.compile, expect further speedups but maintain parity across models when comparing

- Statistical reporting
  - Report mean±std across seeds; use paired t-tests for LM eval tasks when possible. Provide confidence intervals for perplexity differences using block bootstrap over validation batches

```python
def integrate_theoretical_flops(active_layers_schedule, d_model, d_ff, n_heads, seq_len, tokens_per_step):
    total = 0
    for active_layers in active_layers_schedule:  # list per step or per phase
        per_tok = estimate_flops_per_token(d_model, d_ff, n_heads, seq_len, active_layers)
        total += per_tok * tokens_per_step
    return total
```

----------------------------------------
The three experiments—(1) end-to-end head-to-head, (2) ablations/schedule sensitivity, and (3) hardware/quantization/fine-tuning—jointly validate that PLAD-T delivers ≥40% pretraining FLOPs savings without harming downstream quality and with unchanged inference cost. The provided PyTorch-first code skeletons rely on existing, battle-tested libraries (Transformers, PEFT, torch.ao.quantization, lm-eval, torch.profiler) to maximize reliability and ease of reproduction. By integrating activation, self-distillation, and adapter merging into a standard HF training loop, PLAD-T remains hardware-agnostic and PyTorch-friendly while materially reducing end-to-end training compute.

def set_seed(seed: int = 42):

    np.random.seed(seed)

def device_auto():

def causal_mask(sz: int, device: torch.device):
    # returns additive mask (float) with -inf above diagonal
    mask = torch.full((sz, sz), float("-inf"), device=device)
    mask = torch.triu(mask, diagonal=1)

class SyntheticTextDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
